newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Markets set to decline after Fed move.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Markets set to decline after Fed move.

text.p: Major government bond markets are set for fresh declines as the harsh reality of a U.S. interest rate rise, and prospects for further tightenings, begin to sink in, analysts said on Wednesday.

The 25 basis point federal funds increase prompted a selloff in the U.S. led by the short end, which also came under pressure from supply with a two-year auction. Analysts said Bunds would follow the the U.S. but renewed mark strength could help them.
"I am getting a bit negative," said Kirit Shah, chief strategist at Sanwa International in London.
"I don't think there is going to be a collapse. It will just be a gradual decline."
He said the worry for bond markets was that there was no indication from the Fed that this was a one-off rate rise.
The Fed raised its federal funds target rate by 0.25 percent to 5.50 percent.

A statement issued after the Federal Open Market Committee meeting said, "This action was taken in light of persisting strength in demand, which is progressively increasing the risk of inflationary imbalances developing in the economy that would eventually undermine the long expansion."
"The market doesn't like that and is already beginning to price in another hike in the medium term," Shah said.
"If the U.S. market falls further, it is going to be dragged down by the short end's performance and Bunds are going to struggle to remain above par." he said.
Michael Burke, bond strategist at Citibank in London, saw the yield on the U.S. long bond going to 7.50 percent.
At 1005 GMT, the 30-year benchmark bond was at 95-23 to yield 6.97 percent.
"There has been a lot of misplaced optimism that the long end would rally on a tightening which would be an unprecedented event," Burke said.
Andrew Bevan, senior bond economist at Goldman Sachs in London agreed there was likely to be some further deterioration.

"At the longer end of the market, the 30-year might take some comfort from the fact that this is a pre-emptive move but on anything beyond a one to two month view bonds are likely to trade up into the 7.25 percent area," he said.
Shah said the only thing that could help Treasuries to rally would be soft data or a significant slow down in economic growth in the medium term.
Elsewhere, analysts said the fall in bond markets was likely to be limited.
"There has already been an unwinding in the bond price bubble in Europe," said Burke.
Bevan said while there was a linkage with Treasuries, there was little likelihood of monetary tightening at any time soon either in Germany or Japan.

"In Germany...the 10-year bond could move into the 6.0 to 6.25 percent range," he said. "But given how much the market has already sold off we would not have an aggressively bearish stance from here."
He advised investors to remain short but to look to protect the profits they have already secured. The 10-year benchmark Bund is currently at 100.63 yielding 5.91 percent.

In Japan, analysts said JGBs were likely to hold their current levels. Earlier Bank of Japan governor Yasuo Matsushita said Japanese monetary policy was strengthening the basis for economic recovery, and JGBs rallied.
"The economy might well soften a little near term on the back of the tax increases that are being implemented. It is tough to be negative on JGBs for the moment," said Bevan.
"JGBs might tread water because Japanese investors could be disinclined to be sellers and move money overseas while other major bond markets look to be in trouble," said Burke.
--Deepthi Wickremasinghe, Bonds Unit +44 171 542 4041
